newsitem.title: CROATIA: Top Croatian ministers visit rebel Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: Top Croatian ministers visit rebel Serb enclave.

text.p: A delegation of top government ministers visited Croatia's last rebel Serb enclave on Tuesday to underscore that Eastern Slavonia's return to Croatian rule would be completed by mid-July.

State radio said Defence Minister Gojko Susak, Interior Minister Ivan Penic and the head of Croatian intelligence service, Miroslav Tudjman, held talks in Eastern Slavonia with U.S. General Jacques Klein.

Klein heads the 5,000-strong U.N. Mission (UNTAES) overseeing the area's gradual return to Croatia from which it seceded in 1991 when Zagreb sought independence from federal Yugoslavia. Its mandate expires on July 15.

Tudjman is the son of Croatia's strongman President Franjo Tudjman, while Susak is a prominent rightist figure within the ruling nationalist HDZ party. They did not meet any Serb representatives during the brief visit.

Last week Croatia proposed a package of human and minority rights for the Serbs, giving them a two-year exemption from service in the Croatian army and right to vote in areas where they lived before the war.
The Serbs dismissed the package as unsatisfactory, demanding that the enclave remained a single administrative unit and not divided in two counties as envisaged by the Croatian constitution.
Susak said Croatia was not ready for further negotiations.

"There are not even theoretical chances there could be other solutions than what has been offered. We have ways and means to carry it out and it's in the interest of Serbs to cooperate and become full-fledged citizens," he told state radio.
Local and regional elections throughout Croatia are scheduled on March 16. Eastern Slavonian Serbs will take part in the voting for the first time since their 1991 rebellion.
Croatian, Serb and UNTAES officials recently carried out another census to find out who would be eligible to vote in the March 16 election.

But it is still unclear exactly how many of some 120,000 Serbs currently living in Eastern Slavonia will vote in March. About half of them are Serb refugees from other rebel enclaves Zagreb recaptured militarily in 1995.

Susak said the pre-war 1991 census would be fully respected in the voting. Interior minister Penic said the 1991 ethnic breakdown would be the basis for a multinational police force which would come under Croatian control on May 1.
"We shall insist on including members of other ethnicities in the police -- Hungarians, Czechs and Slovaks," Penic said, adding the Serbs would constitute up to one third of the force.
He also said Croatia would start controlling the Danube river which skirts the enclave's eastern border with Yugoslavia on February 15.
